title: Honoring the elders
hookLine: he is not one of us who shows no mercy to the young and no respect to the old

cards: "Fie." That's the word Pickthall chose, in his translation of the Qur'an, for a small sound of irritation. A sigh with a word in it.
The kind of noise that slips out when an aging parent asks the same question for the third time, or takes too long at the door, or tells the story you've heard before.
The Qur'an, in surah Bani Isra'il, forbids exactly that sound. Not shouting. Not cruelty.
Just the little huff. That's how close the line is drawn around the old.

teach.b: Here are the words, in Pickthall's translation of 17:23: "If one of them or both of them attain old age with thee, say not "Fie" unto them nor repulse them, but speak unto them a gracious word." With thee.
Some readers hear in that a parent growing old in your house, in your care.

The next verse adds the posture: lower to them the wing of humility, out of mercy, and pray for them, as they cared for you when you were little. Then the hadith widens the circle from parents to every elder.

In al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: he is not one of us who does not show mercy to our young and does not honor our old. Not one of us. Strong words, set beside ordinary acts.
And a hadith in Abu Dawud goes further: honoring a gray-haired Muslim is part of glorifying Allah.

teach.h: GRAY HAIR, A REASON FOR RESPECT.
teach.b: Gray hair, in that picture, isn't something to hide or hurry past. It's a reason for respect. Notice how the Tirmidhi hadith holds the young and the old together.
Mercy goes down, to the small. Honor goes up, to the old. And the person in the middle of life, busy, tired, impatient, is the one being spoken to.
The elder at the end of the table may be slow. The verse doesn't ask you to pretend otherwise. It asks for the gracious word anyway.

how: Muslims are taught to honor parents and elders, citing surah 17:23–24 and hadith that honoring the old is part of glorifying Allah, and treat visiting and serving elders as part of the faith.

o: no sigh at the old; a gracious word and a lowered wing
obeying any older person, whatever they ask of you
caring for parents only once they can no longer walk

games.q: honoring the elders — tap the pairs.

s: the verse forbids only shouting at old parents
it forbids even saying "Fie" to them, and asks for a gracious word.
the hadith in al-Tirmidhi pairs mercy to the young with honor to the old
he is not one of us who does neither.
a hadith in Abu Dawud links honoring a gray-haired Muslim to glorifying Allah
gray hair is a reason for respect.

games.q: your aging parent asks the same question for the third time. what does the verse ask of you?
o: a quiet sigh, but answer anyway.
remind them gently that they asked already.
games.why: surah 17:23: say not "Fie" unto them nor repulse them, but speak unto them a gracious word.

practice: Bring to mind someone older in your life: a parent, a grandparent, an old neighbor, a retired teacher, someone at the mosque or down the hall.
Think of one question to ask them about their own life, and picture listening to the whole answer, even if you've heard it before. If you pray, remember them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Honoring the elders. No sigh, no brushing off; the gracious word, the lowered wing, respect for the gray hair. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the small sound of irritation in 17:23, which Pickthall renders "Fie".

carryVoice: Your line: honor the gray hair. The gracious word, even when they're slow. Thanks for sitting with this one.

sources.q: If one of them or both of them attain old age with thee, say not "Fie" unto them nor repulse them, but speak unto them a gracious word.
